content.rendered:
I played my last college baseball game just a few days ago, and honestly, it didn’t hit me until I realized I had no practice to go to today. Here is what’s on my mind. By no means is this an exhaustive list of what I’ve taken away from the game, but here goes:

I love baseball, and my appreciation for the game has only grown year by year. It is such a simple game. That is not to say it isn’t difficult—it’s incredibly hard. It will knock you down more often than it builds you up. You will struggle, but you will also thrive. This game will break your heart at times, but it teaches you how to show up again the next day. That is where you find the most joy: in the process, the adjustment and the “figuring things out.” Don’t ever stop learning; that’s when you lose the most valuable part of the game. Always err on the side of aggressiveness. And most importantly, always be yourself out there.

This is all easy to say in theory. The reality is that you will sometimes get lost in the results—the wins and losses, the pressure—and you may find that you’ve lost sight of why you started playing in the first place.

We all want to win championships and get the big hit, but that’s not why we started. We started because the neighbor kid asked us to join their Wiffle Ball game. Because we loved the way the bat sat in our fingers right before we mustered a big swing. Maybe it was because, somewhere, sometime, somebody yelled “RUN!” after we made contact for the first time, and it became instinct. 

We played because we felt free, running like the wind around those bases. And we felt part of something cool when we scooted out of the dugout as fast as our little legs could go because our coach told us to hustle everywhere. We played because we figured out that if we threw the ball hard enough, the glove made a loud POP! We played because we almost got the ball to our right after making a full extension dive and landing hard on our stomachs, only to get up and taste gritty sand in our teeth — we would get the next one though. We knew we’d get the next one.

And that is why we continued: because we knew if we worked hard enough, we could catch that next one. We fell in love with the growth. We watched how effortless the older kids looked, and we wanted to be like them. We found pleasure in the grind because it got us one step closer to that next diving play to our right.

But unfortunately, there is not always a next one. One day, you’ll stand up and wipe the dust off of your jersey, and that will be the last time you get dirty. You’ll sprint out to your position for the last time. Dig into the box for the last time. Dig in your glove for that slider for the last time. Turn that ground ball into two outs for the last time. You may not know it then, but that last time will come and go. 

I’m going to miss whipping the ball across the diamond and the excitement of any ball hit in my general direction. I’m going to miss rounding first base hard after a low line drive sneaks through the infield. I’m going to miss flying around the bases to score from first when a teammate crushes one in the gap and then high-fiving the whole dugout while catching my breath. I’m going to miss saying “Let’s go win a ball game” before hustling out for the top of the ninth. These little moments—and the people who shared them—are what made it special.

So savor the journey; that is the real prize. Maybe you’ll remember the big games, the strikeouts, the trophies. But you’ll more likely remember the hard work, your love for the game and the relationships you build along the way. You’ll remember the coach who wanted you to succeed more than anything, the teammate who kept you confident and loose and the people who rearranged their lives just to get you to the field. 

You’ll remember your bus buddy for away games and even the goofy kid you played summer ball with for only ten games. And you’ll remember that teacher you bonded with over your love for baseball. You probably won’t remember every inside joke or dugout quote you enjoyed with your teammates. But you’ll sure remember how being together with them in that dugout and running out to the field together made you feel. So remember to thank those who made your journey possible. I will never forget the gratitude I felt the moment I realized how lucky I was to play this game with the support of the people I love. It brings a smile to my face and fills my heart.

And one more thing: don’t ever give up. You never know what opportunity awaits if you relentlessly continue to learn and love. One day, you’ll realize it has already given you more than you ever could have asked for.

Andrew Sellers ’26 is a senior biology major and a member of the Carleton men’s baseball team.
